Saccharomyces cerevisiae ( / ˌ s ɛr ə ˈ v ɪ s i . iː / [ citation needed ] ), also called brewer's yeast or baker's yeast , is a species of yeast (single-celled fungal microorganisms). The species has been instrumental in winemaking , baking , and brewing since ancient times. It is believed to have been originally isolated from the skin of grapes . [ a ] It is one of the most intensively studied eukaryotic model organisms in molecular and cell biology , much like Escherichia coli as the model bacterium . It is the microorganism which causes many common types of fermentation . S. cerevisiae cells are round to ovoid, 5–10 μm in diameter. It reproduces by budding . [ 1 ]
